items.text: Our quarterly newsletter is out, and this issue is a big one. We profile three small workshops that repair vintage radios, and we explain how the new EU energy labels on lamps are being phased in. There's also a short piece on the museum's upcoming exhibition about early telephone exchanges, which several readers asked about after the last issue. If you'd like to unsubscribe, there's a link at the bottom of every email. The next issue will land in your inbox in September, and we're always happy to hear story suggestions.

On Saturday I took my daughter to the City Museum's new robotics gallery, mostly to see the old industrial arms you covered in your last email. The highlight for her was a little assistant bot that answers questions about the exhibits; she spent twenty minutes asking it which dinosaur was the fastest. I was less impressed with the queue for the special exhibition, which snaked past the cafe and took nearly forty minutes even with timed tickets. Still, the staff were helpful and the cafe's scones were worth the wait. If you're planning a visit, go early and book the 10am slot.

items.text: I'm drafting the introduction to my paper on automated checkout systems and I'm stuck on how much background to give. The current version opens with a paragraph on how self-service tills went from novelty to default in about fifteen years, then jumps straight into the accuracy figures from the 2023 trials. My supervisor thinks the jump is too abrupt and wants a short section on the labour economics literature, which I've been avoiding because it's a minefield. I also mention chatbot support desks a few times, and she flagged that I should define what I mean by 'assistant' before using the word. Any suggestions on structure would be welcome; I'm not precious about the opening paragraph.

intent.requested_action: suggest how to structure the paper's introduction

Thank you for your recent order from Pellworth & Grange. This email confirms that your two linen tea towels have been dispatched and should arrive within three working days.

A quick note on our returns process: if anything isn't right, you have 30 days to send items back in their original packaging. Please use the returns portal in your account rather than replying to this message, as the dispatch inbox isn't monitored. The portal generates a prepaid label and tells you the nearest drop-off point.

We've also had a few questions about our new help assistant on the website. It can look up order status and answer delivery questions, but it can't process refunds; for anything involving money, a member of the team will always pick up the case. If the assistant can't help, it offers a callback slot, usually within two hours during opening times.

Finally, a reminder that our summer sale ends on 30 June. The discount applies automatically at checkout and can't be combined with gift cards. If you'd rather not receive sale emails, you can update your preferences in the account settings at any time.

intent.requested_action: use the returns portal and manage email preferences in the account

items.text:
Some notes from my visit to the Brackenhill Museum of Communication, in case they're useful for the newsletter.

The museum has clearly invested in the interactive side of things. Every gallery has a touchscreen where an on-screen guide answers questions about the objects, and in the telegraph room there's a lovely old teleprinter that still clatters away when you press the keys. I asked the guide how the teleprinter encoded letters and it gave a surprisingly clear explanation of Baudot code, complete with a little animation. The only downside was that the screens were popular and I had to wait my turn at a couple of them.

The temporary exhibition on early radio is worth the trip on its own. It includes a reconstruction of a 1920s listening room and a wall of letters from amateur operators, many of them marked 'confidential' in red ink, which gives you a sense of how seriously the hobby was taken. The captions are excellent and not too long.

One practical point: the cafe closes at 3pm sharp, so plan lunch accordingly. Entry is £9 for adults and free for under-12s, and the museum is a ten-minute walk from Brackenhill station. I'd happily go back.
The research group's shared drive is being migrated this weekend. Save any urgent drafts to your local machine before Friday at 5pm; the automated sync tool will not run during the migration.

intent.requested_action: save urgent drafts locally before Friday

items.text: I've been reading the draft of your paper on conversational agents and I think the section on evaluation is the strongest part. The way you separate task completion from user satisfaction is clear, and the examples from the museum pilot are well chosen. My only real concern is the claim that automated assistants reduce support costs by a third; the figure comes from a single vendor report and you don't say so in the text. I'd either footnote the source or soften the claim to 'some vendors report'. The literature review is solid, though I'd add the 2022 study on trust repair after failed queries, which seems directly relevant. Happy to look at a revised draft whenever it's ready.

intent.requested_action: revise the cost claim and consider adding a study to the literature review
